A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same survey and retain its central taxonomy. All 26 pages of v2 and 28 pages of v3 support comparison, including v3's appendices. V2 ends with references and has no appendix.

before.justification: Figure 1 reports descriptive publication counts and annual method/attribute statistics compiled for the survey. These constitute original bibliometric data analysis, although v2 reports no original TTS benchmark experiments.

after.justification: V3 retains Figure 1's descriptive statistics and adds original synthesis experiments and comparisons with human ratings in Appendix A.5, Tables 6–7.

M1.justification: Section 4.2.2 and Appendix A.5 introduce a Gemini-based evaluator that takes synthesized audio, its transcript, and an instruction, then produces three rubric-guided scores. V2 proposes no corresponding evaluation procedure. This addition concerns speech assessment; the surveyed synthesis systems are not newly redesigned.

E1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds English and Chinese zero-shot and description/instruction-based synthesis evaluations. It uses MSP-Podcast and Emo-Emilia reference utterances and generated textual instructions. These actual evaluations are absent from v2; the retained dataset catalogue alone does not establish experimental coverage.

E2.justification: Table 7 newly compares the proposed evaluator against NISQA and UTMOS. Table 6 also introduces empirical comparisons among open-source and commercial TTS systems. Its instruction-based results include EmoVoice, whereas the implementation list names PromptTTS instead; PromptTTS has no reported result row.

E3.justification: The new protocol specifies 20 samples per model/task, divided equally between English and Chinese, three evaluation dimensions scored from 1 to 5, and a separate 96-sample comparison with human ratings. These are new experimental settings, not revisions of a corresponding v2 benchmark.

E4.justification: Beyond reporting TTS scores, Appendix A.5.3 adds a focused evaluator-reliability analysis: whether automated judgments track human ratings across 96 synthesized samples. It compares Pearson correlations for Gemini, NISQA, and UTMOS. No ablations or sensitivity studies are added.

E5.justification: Table 6 introduces score summaries with ± quantities, and Appendix A.5.3 introduces Pearson-correlation estimation. The PDF does not define the ± quantities or provide repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Additional independent runs therefore cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Tables 6–7 add previously absent results. Vevo leads zero-shot naturalness at 4.43±0.55, while CosyVoice leads instruction following at 4.81±0.28. The proposed evaluator's human correlations are 0.12, 0.17, and 0.14. These are new results, not same-setting improvements over v2.

T1.justification: Equations 1–2 replace v2's conditional-probability equalities with incomplete expressions beginning with arg max over model parameters. These alter the mathematical formulation and are ill-formed as printed. The standard metric formulas, Equations 3–10, survive in Appendix A.4; no proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central claim of providing the first comprehensive controllable-TTS survey and taxonomy remains. V3 narrows the explicitly promised background and impact coverage, while Appendix A.5.4 adds a preliminary claim that its MLLM evaluator can predict human-aligned scores.

C2.justification: V3 adds architecture and control-strategy trend analyses, explicit disentanglement mechanisms, control-strategy trade-offs, survey limitations, and interpretations of the Gemini experiments. V2's detailed generalization, efficiency, and security discussions are substantially reduced or removed. These change the substantive discussion beyond reorganizing it.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 supplies sample allocations, reference datasets, the full evaluator prompt and scoring rubric, and bilingual synthesis instructions. Section 8 newly discloses literature-search sources and ChatGPT assistance. Existing resource links remain, but checkpoints, human-rating procedures, and the meaning of ± remain unspecified.

R1.justification: V3 substantially prunes foundational TTS, vocoder, generalization, and security references, while adding disentanglement and automated-evaluation literature, including SpeechTripleNet, APG-MOS, NISQA, UTMOS, and EmoVoice. The first-survey positioning remains, but the reviewed literature changes substantially beyond citation-style and publication-metadata updates.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the body are extensively condensed and rewritten. V3 introduces a task-focused organization, restructures method discussions, moves retained background and metric explanations into appendices, and adds research-trend, limitations, and ethics sections.

P2.justification: V2's separate method Tables III–IV become the much denser Table 1. Several catalogues and the pipeline figure move to the appendix, and the control-strategy table is redesigned. Challenge/future-direction figures disappear; an architecture-evolution diagram, prompt panel, and two experimental tables are added.

improvement.justification: V3 improves task organization and makes control-strategy trade-offs explicit, while adding exploratory empirical evidence. However, Appendix A.5 contains a model-roster conflict and ambiguous score reporting. Its three-dimension superiority claim lacks instruction-following comparator results in Table 7, and human correlations are only 0.12–0.17. Equations 1–2 become ill-formed, and the merged method table is harder to read. These benefits and harms do not establish a reliable net quality direction.
